## "Go find out. Actually find out."

That's what you told the systems administrator three modules ago, when `breach-notification-and-
dual-reporting` left the Brookfield laptop in exactly the state 164.402's presumption leaves
anything it can't rebut: treated as a breach, provisionally, until someone brings back a better
answer. He's back now, with your Quality Analyst (QA) beside him, and a folder of exactly what
he found — enrollment logs, a vendor support ticket, a network log excerpt, and one short,
useless interview.

"I want to be straight with you before you read any of it," he says. "I did everything I know
how to do. I don't have a clean answer. I have a better-documented version of the same unknown."

That sentence is this module's whole job, stated honestly before a single page gets turned.
Not every investigation ends with a flipped verdict. Some end exactly where they started, with
a thicker file proving the organization actually looked. Your job today is to read that file the
way an OCR (the HHS Office for Civil Rights) investigator eventually might, decide whether it
changes anything module 4 locked, find the actual root cause underneath all of it, and close
this course with whatever honest answer the facts support — not the one that would look best in
a slide.

## Why this step exists, and the ITSM bridge

Every prior module in this course was about a rule and a test: who may see PHI (protected
health information), what has to guard it, whether a presumption gets rebutted. This module is
about something ITSM (IT service management) already has a name for, even though HIPAA's text
never uses it: **problem management**. An incident gets contained and a workaround gets applied
long before anyone knows the actual root cause. Problem management is the separate discipline
that keeps digging after the fire's out — not to change what already happened, but to find the
underlying condition that let it happen, log it in a known-error record, and decide whether a
permanent fix is worth building.

HIPAA doesn't hand you a section titled "root cause analysis." What it hands you instead is
164.414(b)'s burden of proof: Lakeshore has to demonstrate either that every required
notification was made, or that the event wasn't a breach at all. You cannot demonstrate either
one by shrugging. You demonstrate it by actually investigating — pulling every log that might
exist, escalating to the people who hold data you don't, interviewing the person who was there —
and writing down what you found, including what you tried and still couldn't find. The failure
mode this module guards against isn't "the investigation reached an unsatisfying conclusion."
It's "nobody can show their work," which is a different and much worse problem to have in front
of a regulator who has the burden of proof sitting squarely on you.

## The rule in plain English

There's no new regulation to read today. This module's job is to apply, honestly and in order,
everything the first four already built: re-open the encryption question module 1 logged and
module 3 and 4 couldn't close, dig as far as a real investigation can actually dig, and then
re-run — not re-litigate — 164.402's four-factor test with whatever the dig actually produced.
If new facts change a factor, the determination can change. If the dig comes up empty, the
determination module 4 reached stands, now as this course's **final** answer instead of a
provisional one — and 164.414(b)'s burden of proof means Lakeshore still has to be able to show,
on paper, that it tried.

## The actual text, reused

All quotes below are verbatim from the same saved files modules 3 and 4 already quoted in full —
`sources/cfr/45-164-security-rule-excerpt.md` and `sources/cfr/45-164-breach-notification-
excerpt.md`. Nothing here is new; it's reproduced only where this module leans on it directly.

> **164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D):** Information system activity review (Required). Implement procedures
> to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports,
> and security incident tracking reports.

> **164.402(2)(iii):** Whether the protected health information was actually acquired or
> viewed[.]

> **164.414(b):** [T]he covered entity or business associate, as applicable, shall have the
> burden of demonstrating that all notifications were made as required by this subpart or that
> the use or disclosure did not constitute a breach, as defined at § 164.402.

Read those three together and the module's whole shape is right there. 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) is
the Required specification this investigation is, belatedly, finally satisfying for this one
device. 164.402(2)(iii) is the single factor the whole course has been circling since module 3.
164.414(b) is why "we tried and couldn't tell" has to be a documented finding, not a verbal
shrug.

## The investigation — what the systems administrator actually did

Four separate leads. Walk each one the way the folder on your desk lays them out.

**1. Enrollment and policy-push logs.** The device-management platform's own enrollment record
confirms, cleanly, what module 3 already said could be confirmed: the laptop enrolled under
Lakeshore's full-disk-encryption policy, and the policy profile pushed successfully at
enrollment. That much was never actually in doubt. It answers "was the device told to encrypt
itself," not "did it."

**2. Check-in history, read more carefully than the surface-level status field.** Here's where
the systems administrator went past where module 3 stopped. The laptop was issued shortly
before the device-management platform migration — which means its entire operating life, before
the loss, sits almost entirely inside the migration window. Pulling the raw check-in history
instead of trusting the dashboard's single "not reported" field, he found only two check-ins
ever logged for this specific device before the migration cutover. Both show the encryption
policy as assigned. Neither shows a completed encryption-status attestation.

That's a real, structural reason, not a shrug: on this platform's architecture, encryption
attestation runs as a background compliance scan that doesn't finish on a device's first one or
two check-ins after imaging — it needs an idle window the device apparently never had, because
it went straight from imaging into travel service for the Brookfield review. The "not reported"
field isn't only a migration artifact. It may be that no attestation had ever completed, on
either platform, before the device went missing. The migration didn't necessarily erase a known
answer. It may have cut off the only chance for an answer to ever get recorded.

**3. Vendor escalation.** The systems administrator opened a case with the device-management
platform's vendor and asked them to check their own backend telemetry — the raw data their
servers receive, not just what the admin console surfaces. Two findings came back. First, the
vendor confirmed a known defect class in their migration tooling: devices with fewer than a
handful of check-ins at cutover could lose in-progress compliance-attribute data during the
account remap, which is consistent with, though doesn't fully prove, what happened here. Second,
and more final: the old platform was already decommissioned on its own retention schedule before
this investigation began, and its last full data export — the one place a late-arriving
attestation might have been archived — was already purged under that same routine schedule. If
anything more existed, it's no longer retrievable from either side.

**4. Network logs, and the one human being who was there.** The central site's meeting-room
network — the one the Brookfield staff member's laptop connected to on the day of the
presentation, its last confirmed network session before the loss — is a visitor-segment network
that doesn't run device posture or compliance checks on anything that joins it. No attestation
exists from that connection either, by design, not by oversight anyone can fix retroactively.
And the staff member, interviewed directly, isn't a technical employee and genuinely doesn't
remember ever seeing an encryption indicator, a prompt, or anything else that would help either
way. That's not evasiveness. It's an honest "I wasn't looking for that, and I had no reason to."

**One thread did close.** Module 4 left an open action item: confirm whether a remote
lock-or-wipe command was actually issued through the device-management platform when the loss
was reported, not merely assumed. It was issued — the systems administrator can show the
command's timestamp and status in the platform's own log. What the log also shows, honestly, is
that the command has never been marked delivered, because a lock or wipe command can only reach
a device that comes back online, and this one hasn't. Issuance is now a confirmed fact. Receipt
is not, and structurally may never be confirmable unless the device itself resurfaces.

## The honest conclusion: this cannot be resolved

Four leads, four dead ends, each explained by something real rather than a failure to look.
There is no last-known-good encryption reading to recover, because the device's whole short life
sits inside a window where no platform — old or new — ever completed its first confirmation, and
the one record that might have captured a late one no longer exists. This is not the same
finding as "encryption was off." It is also not "encryption was confirmed on." It is a genuine,
permanent unknown, and per this curriculum's own working rule — stated honestly, not dressed up
as a cleaner finding than it is — that unknown stays an unknown.

## Root cause — reasoning through which gap actually matters most

Three real gaps sit behind this incident. Naming all three without picking one and calling it
done would be the easy, lazy version of this section. Here's the reasoning, in order of how
directly each one explains what actually happened.

**The proximate cause of the loss itself: a physical-handling gap.** Nothing downstream in this
course happens if the laptop never leaves the staff member's hand. A shoulder bag, set down
unattended in the back seat of a shared ride, with no second control — no cable lock, no
"carry-on only" habit, no reflex to keep the bag in sight between a meeting and a gate — is a
training and process gap, plain and simple. This is the thing a CAPA (corrective and preventive
action)-style fix should target directly: a concrete handling rule for devices carrying BECS
(Blood Establishment Computer Software) extracts off-site, reinforced the way any workforce
security-awareness control under 164.308(a)(5) would be.

**The reason the compliance question can never close: a deployment-sequencing gap.** This is the
root cause this module's own digging actually surfaced, and it's the one worth fixing first,
because it's structural and will recur. A freshly imaged device went straight into travel
service before its first encryption attestation had time to complete — and then a platform
migration permanently cut off any later chance to backfill that confirmation. The fix isn't "be
more careful during the next migration." It's a standing rule: a newly enrolled device doesn't
leave the building for field or travel use until its first compliance attestation has actually
completed and been confirmed, migration or no migration. That single rule would have prevented
today's unresolved question regardless of whether the laptop had ever been lost at all, which is
exactly the kind of fix 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D)'s "regularly review" standard is meant to produce —
not a review that happens after the device is already gone.

**The gap that made the exposure worse than it needed to be: the minimum-necessary gap.**
`the-hipaa-privacy-rule` already found this, independently of everything above: three of the
extract's six fields — name, date of birth, lifetime donation count — never needed to ride
along. That gap didn't cause the loss and didn't cause the encryption question to go unanswered.
What it did was guarantee that if this device's contents were ever acquired or viewed, the
record exposed was bigger and more re-identifiable than the review ever required. A standing
report template scoped to actual need, per 164.514(d)(3)(i)'s own requirement, would have made
every future version of this exact incident smaller, regardless of what happens to any specific
laptop.

Ranked honestly: the physical-handling gap is what triggered this specific event, but the
deployment-sequencing gap is the one that most directly explains why today's question can never
be answered — and it's the one most likely to produce the identical unresolved finding again,
on a different device, the next time a migration or a rushed deployment collides with a new
enrollment. Fix the sequencing gap, and the organization at least gets a clean yes-or-no answer
next time, even if the device still gets lost. The minimum-necessary gap doesn't explain this
incident's facts at all, but it's the one multiplier sitting quietly under every version of this
story, making each one worse than it had to be.

## Closing the four-factor assessment — the final determination

Re-run module 4's own test, factor by factor, against what this module actually found.

**Factor 1 (nature and extent of the PHI).** Unchanged. The six-field extract is still what it
was — still a meaningful re-identification risk. Nothing this investigation found touches this
factor.

**Factor 2 (who received it).** Unchanged. Still unknown. No lead above identified a recipient.

**Factor 3 (was it actually acquired or viewed) — the one factor this entire investigation was
built to resolve.** It remains unresolved, now for a documented, structural reason instead of a
simple "migration broke the field": no attestation ever completed on this device, on either
platform, and no corroborating record exists anywhere else that could substitute for one. An
unresolved factor still cannot rebut a presumption. Nothing about having a thicker, more honest
file changes that math.

**Factor 4 (mitigation).** Slightly more resolved than before. The remote wipe command is now
confirmed **issued**, closing module 4's open action item — but confirmed **not delivered**,
because the device has never come back online to receive it. Real mitigation effort, genuinely
undercut by a device that simply isn't reachable.

**The final determination.** Four factors, and factor 3 — the pivotal one — is exactly where
module 4 left it, now for a fully investigated reason instead of an open question. 164.402(2)'s
presumption of breach was not rebutted in module 4, and it is **still not rebutted today.**
There is no new fact strong enough to change that. **Module 4's provisional breach determination
is now this course's final one.** Individual notification under 164.404 proceeds on the clock
that already started the day the loss was reported — this investigation, run over roughly the
weeks since, has not reset or extended that clock, and notifications are being finalized on
schedule, not delayed to wait for an answer that was never going to arrive. 164.406 media
notification stays not triggered; 164.408(c)'s under-500 annual-log pathway still applies. None
of module 4's mapped obligations change. What changes is only this: Lakeshore can now show,
on paper, that it did not simply assume this answer — it looked, documented four real attempts,
and can prove exactly why each one came up empty. That file is what 164.414(b)'s burden of proof
actually demands, and it's a materially stronger position than "we don't know" ever was, even
though the bottom-line determination is identical.

## What an inspector or reviewer would actually look for

An OCR investigator, or an AABB (the Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies)
assessor asking how Lakeshore handled a device loss, wouldn't be satisfied by the determination
alone. They'd ask for this investigation's actual record: the enrollment log, the raw check-in
history (not just the dashboard summary), the vendor case number and its written response, the
network-segment finding, and a dated note of the staff interview — plus the remote-wipe command's
issued-but-undelivered status, timestamped. A weak answer sounds like "we couldn't confirm
encryption, so we treated it as a breach." A credible answer produces the file above, factor by
factor, showing exactly what was tried and why each avenue closed. 164.414(b) puts the burden on
Lakeshore; an investigator who asks "show me you actually looked" and gets this file has nothing
left to cite.

## Common traps

**"We couldn't resolve it, so the investigation failed."** No. An investigation that
documents four genuine, structurally-explained dead ends and closes one real open item (the
wipe command) is a successful investigation with an unresolved finding — a different thing
entirely from an investigation nobody bothered to run. 164.414(b) doesn't require a resolved
answer. It requires a demonstrated one, and "we tried everything available and here's exactly
why none of it worked" is a demonstrated answer.

**"The notifications already went out, so the matter is closed."** Notification discharges
164.404's obligation. It doesn't discharge the organization's separate obligation to fix what
actually let this happen. The deployment-sequencing gap this module found doesn't go away
because 212 donors got a letter — it's still sitting there, ready to produce the identical
unresolved finding on the next device that gets imaged, deployed, and lost inside a migration
window.

## What this means for your job

- **Know the difference between "we assumed" and "we investigated and couldn't confirm."**
  164.414(b) only rewards the second one. If your systems administrator ever hands you a
  conclusion without a file behind it, that's the question to ask before you sign off on
  anything.
- **Treat an unresolved factor as a finished finding, not an open task waiting on someone else.**
  Once every reasonable lead has been run down and documented, "genuinely unknown" is itself the
  answer — don't let your team keep the determination "pending" past the point where pending
  stops meaning anything.
- **Separate root cause from breach determination, and fix the root cause regardless of how the
  determination lands.** This incident's deployment-sequencing gap would be worth fixing even in
  a universe where the presumption had been rebutted. Don't let a favorable breach outcome talk
  your team out of a genuine process fix.
- **Rank candidate root causes instead of listing them.** Your QA and your systems administrator
  will often hand you two or three plausible causes at once. Your job is to ask which one most
  directly explains what happened and which one is most likely to recur — not to accept whichever
  one is handed to you first or feels least embarrassing.
- **Keep the vendor relationship itself on your radar as its own risk, not just a source of
  logs.** The device-management platform's migration is sitting at the center of this entire
  unresolved thread — a vendor's own change, outside Lakeshore's direct control, produced a gap
  Lakeshore now has to live with. That's worth remembering past this course.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator says, "I found a structural reason for every dead end, so I'm confident encryption was actually on." Is that a fair reading of the investigation?

Not quite. Every dead end this module found has a real, honest explanation — but none of them is
evidence that encryption *was* active, only evidence of why no record exists either way. "I can
explain why I don't have proof" is not the same claim as "I have proof." 164.402(2)(iii) asks
whether the PHI was actually acquired or viewed, and the honest answer stays "unresolved," not
"probably fine." Confidence has to come from evidence, not from a satisfying explanation for its
absence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Is running an investigation like this one — enrollment logs, vendor escalation, network logs, an interview — itself something 164.414(b) names as a required step?

No, and this is worth being precise about. 164.414(b)'s actual text requires demonstrating that
notifications were made or that no breach occurred — it never uses the word "investigation" or
lists these specific steps. Running an investigation this thorough is the practical, sensible way
to meet that burden of proof; it's good practice that makes 164.414(b) defensible, not a
citation of its own. Don't let your team describe "we ran a four-part investigation" as if it
were itself a regulatory checkbox — it's the method, not the requirement.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Does confirming the remote-wipe command was issued (even though it was never confirmed delivered) change today's breach determination at all?

No. It closes module 4's own open action item and strengthens factor 4 (mitigation) honestly —
real effort, genuinely undercut by an unreachable device — but factor 4 was never the factor
standing between Lakeshore and rebutting the presumption. Factor 3 was, and still is. A stronger
mitigation story doesn't substitute for an unresolved acquisition-or-viewing question; all four
factors have to support low probability of compromise, and one unresolved pivotal factor is
enough to keep the presumption standing regardless of how well the other three read.
:::

## Where this course ends, and what's still ahead

Five modules ago, this course opened with a question nobody at Lakeshore had ever had to answer
out loud: is a blood center even subject to HIPAA at all? It closes today with that same
organization holding a fully investigated, honestly unresolved incident — and knowing exactly
what it can and can't say about it.

Here's the arc, named once, start to finish. Module 1 reasoned Lakeshore into HIPAA's reach from
160.103's own definitions — not asserted, worked out — and logged this course's one incident: a
Brookfield laptop, a six-field extract, an encryption status nobody could confirm. Module 2 ran
the Privacy Rule against that extract and found a real, independent minimum-necessary gap: three
of six fields that never needed to make the trip. Module 3 placed the Security Rule's
Required-versus-Addressable mechanism against Part 11's all-or-nothing controls, and found
Lakeshore's encryption *policy* sound while its *verification* of this one device was not — a
genuine compliance gap, deliberately kept separate from any breach question. Module 4 took that
unresolved verification gap into 164.402's actual four-factor test and reached an honest,
provisional conclusion: the presumption of breach was not rebutted, with factor 3 — was the PHI
actually acquired or viewed — as the single pivot point everything else turned on. And this
module sent someone to go find out, as far as a real investigation can go, and came back with an
honestly thicker, better-documented version of the exact same unknown.

Say plainly what's resolved now. The minimum-necessary finding is closed and logged. The
Security Rule's Required-versus-Addressable mechanism is fully understood, with its one genuine
Part 11 difference named and held to. The remote-wipe command's issuance is confirmed. The root
cause is identified and ranked — a deployment-sequencing gap, ahead of a physical-handling gap,
ahead of a severity-multiplying minimum-necessary gap — and the first one comes with a concrete,
fixable rule: no newly enrolled device leaves the building for field service before its first
compliance attestation completes. And the determination itself is final: this incident is a
reportable breach, individual notification proceeding on 164.404's clock, HHS notification on
164.408(c)'s under-500 pathway, no BPDR (Biological Product Deviation Report) independently
triggered.

Say plainly, too, what stays open by honest design, the same way this curriculum has closed
every other course. The Brookfield laptop's encryption status at the moment it went missing will
likely never be known. That is not a loose end this course failed to tie off — it's the
documented, structurally-explained limit of what an investigation can actually recover once a
device's own history and a vendor's retention schedule have both already moved on. A tidier
ending was available if this module had invented a convenient recovered log. It wasn't used,
because this curriculum's whole credibility rests on reporting what an investigation actually
finds, not what would read better.

Two courses ahead pick up exactly where this one stops. `vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`
turns the same scrutiny this module aimed at four internal leads outward, onto the
device-management platform's own vendor — the same vendor whose migration tooling, retention
schedule, and backend telemetry sat at the center of this entire unresolved thread. Reading that
vendor's own security posture, knowing what its change-notification obligations are, and tiering
that relationship's risk the way you'd tier any other vendor's is the natural next place this
exact incident keeps teaching. And Track 5's capstone, `itsm-for-regulated-blood-services`, is
where this course's own move — treating a breach investigation as problem management, root cause
analysis, and a known-error record instead of a one-off scramble — finally sits next to every
other crosswalk this curriculum has built, in the one language built to survive a conversation
with your CIO and your exec quality council in the same breath.

You came into this course unable to say whether HIPAA even applied to a blood center. You leave
it having run one incident through every subpart this course was built to teach — Privacy,
Security, Breach Notification — and closed it the only honest way a real investigation ever
closes: with a final determination, an identified root cause, and one well-documented unknown
left exactly where the evidence actually ran out.
